messages.author: 484c91357ac83f6b
messages.subject: min max for double
parts:
Pardon if my mistake, but is there any reason for the fact that
min(double, double) and max(double, double) are not in grammar, but
max(int, int) and min(int, int) are?

no matches for function name="min"
arg 0 type=real
arg 1 type=real
available function signatures for min:
0. min(int[1]) : int
1. min(real[1]) : real
2. min(vector) : real
3. min(row vector) : real
4. min(matrix) : real
5. min(int, int) : int

(This is consistent with the manual)

Also, oddly, max(a, b) and min(a, b) functions are actually defined for
doubles only:

namespace stan {
namespace math {
inline double max(const double a, const double b) {
return a > b ? a : b;
}
}
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] min max for double
parts:
Yes, we could add this, but it's a bit subtle to get the
signatures right for promotion. The C++ lib and Stan as it
is now only include these two signatures:

int max(int,int);

double fmax(double,double);

This allows calls to

double fmax(double,int);
double fmax(int,double);
double fmax(int,int);

You'll find it a bit tricky to get the promotions right.
We need to add:

double max(double,double);
double max(int,double);
double max(double,int);
int max(int,int);

I think that'll keep us out of trouble with attempts to
promote (demote) to the int type from double.

- Bob

> 2. min(vector) : real
> 3. min(row vector) : real

>
> (This is consistent with the manual)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] min max for double

Then should I specialize them for var/fvar? Currently, no version of
min/max has specializations for var/fvar, and I really find this reasonable.

But fmax/fmin does:

inline var fmax(const stan::agrad::var& a,
const stan::agrad::var& b) {
return a.vi_->val_ > b.vi_->val_ ? a : b;
}


I find this code strange:

inline var fmax(const stan::agrad::var& a,
const double& b) {
return a.vi_->val_ >= b ? a : var(b);
}

This seems to be a odd case to arise, but if it does, then the gradient
will be carried on if it's greater, otherwise a new var is started, but
is this really a wanted behavior? Or is it better always return a new
var, even if b is higher?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] min max for double
parts: No, they don't need specializations.

On 5/29/13 1:28 AM, Marco Inacio wrote:
> Then should I specialize them for var/fvar?

> Currently, no version of min/max has specializations for var/fvar, and I
> really find this reasonable.

Yes, they're only defined for int. But if we change that,
they'll need to follow fmax.

>
> But fmax/fmin does:
>
> inline var fmax(const stan::agrad::var& a,
> const stan::agrad::var& b) {
> return a.vi_->val_ > b.vi_->val_ ? a : b;
> }

Now that you bring it up, we could return a const reference:

inline var&
fmax(const var& a, const var& b) {
if (a > b)
return a;
else
return b;
}

I'm not sure if you can take a reference through the conditional
operator (a > b ? a : b).

> I find this code strange:
>
> inline var fmax(const stan::agrad::var& a,
> const double& b) {
> return a.vi_->val_ >= b ? a : var(b);
> }
>
> This seems to be a odd case to arise, but if it does, then the gradient will be carried on if it's greater, otherwise a
> new var is started, but is this really a wanted behavior? Or is it better always return a new var, even if b is higher?

We need to support all the polymorphism that's possible
in Stan, so we need to allow this.

You're right about the behavior of the gradient. I
don't see any other alternative. As is, if you have two var inputs,
you lose the gradient info on one of them anyway.

We could try to warn users in the doc. It gets hairy
to start issuing warnings on a per-function, per-argument config
basis.

- Bob

I agree that a change to the manual only should only have to satisfy make manual.

I think it would be better if the .stan code blocks were each separate files that were put into the manual with a \verbatiminput

http://www.tex.ac.uk/cgi-bin/texfaq2html?label=verbfile

That way, we could have a make target to verify that they all parsed (and perhaps compiled). But that would be better than having a misleading manual.

> good bit of tedious work to get them all into shape. But that would be better than having a misleading manual.

That's what I did for our manuals at our company.

The challenge is that they're not whole models, just
fragments. They could be embedded in whole models, but
those shouldn't go in the manual.

I have some pretty robust Java code that I'm happy to share
that cuts out bits of models and includes those. It uses code
comments to indicate where to start/stop and what the name of
the resulting file to include is. Something like:

parameters {
real a;
}
model {
/* start block.tex */
a ~ normal(0,1);
/* end */
}

would print just

a ~ normal(0,1);

I'd probably have to beef it up for some of our special symbols.

Another nice part about it is that it includes only half vertical
lines for empty lines, which helps with clarity without wasting
ridiculous amounts of vertical space.

The only issue is that it'd introduce a Java dependency on making
the manual. And make things that much more complex for everyone
else to understand.

- Bob

I think we're in agreement for Stan. (I was just pointing
out why they are different in C++ and why having the signatures
below isn't exactly equivalent to what we have now.)

Specifically, I'm OK with deprecating fmax() and generalizing max()
to only use the Stan signatures:

int max(int,int);
real max(int,real);
real max(real,int);
real max(real,real);

And similarly for min() vs. fmin().

Here's a nice discussion of the distinction in C++:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/1632145/use-of-min-and-max-functions-in-c

We absolutely need to keep the distinction as-is in the
C++ library for C++ compatibility, but that's a different
issue than keeping it in Stan.

It's going to be tricky, though, with the way Stan compiles.
It will just use max() for max() and it will try to call
the standard libraries unless we're careful to import our own
and our own have better type matches.

> Something similar happens with fabs() and abs():
>
> abs() and fabs() are a confusing case for the user since they are definied together at documentation exactly the same
> way, with the same words and there's no explanation on where one should use each one.

and just go with these:

int abs(int);
real abs(real);

> real abs(real x)
> The absolute value of x
> real fabs(real x)
> The absolute value of x
> (page 199)

I should have never included

real abs(real);

in the first place.

I don't think there is a problem for Stan.

We just have to be careful not to break the
expected C++ behavior in our API. That means leaving
the fmin and fmax functions in place and behaving as
they currently behave.

>> It's going to be tricky, though, with the way Stan compiles.
>> It will just use max() for max() and it will try to call
>> the standard libraries unless we're careful to import our own
>> and our own have better type matches.
>
> I didn't know that, how does this happen? My guess was that there were a "using std;" in Stan compiled code, but I found
> none, so why would it call std::max? Is there a way I could simulate this behavior in a unit test to check which
> function is being called?

This is very confusing in C++.

Check out this description of abs(), with signature

int abs(int);

in <cstdlib>:

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cstdlib/abs/

You don't need an include to compile this program in
file abs.cpp:

#include <iostream>
int main() {
std::cout << "abs(-2.3)=" << abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
}

It has this rather unexpected behavior:

~/temp2$ clang++ abs.cpp
~/temp2$ ./a.out
abs(-2.3)=2

What's happening is that the double value -2.3 is getting
cast to an integer (-2) and then run through abs().

Turns out there's another abs() in <cmath> with three
overloaded signatures. Now compare this program:

#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
int main() {
std::cout << "abs(-2.3)=" << abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
std::cout << "std::abs(-2.3)=" << std::abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
}

which as you might expect does this:

~/temp2$ clang++ abs2.cpp
~/temp2$ ./a.out
abs(-2.3)=2
std::abs(-2.3)=2.3

An explicit "using" seems to force the std::abs version
as seen in abs3.cpp:

#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
int main() {
using std::abs;
std::cout << "abs(-2.3)=" << abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
std::cout << "std::abs(-2.3)=" << std::abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
}

which produces this:

~/temp2$ clang++ abs3.cpp
~/temp2$ ./a.out
abs(-2.3)=2.3
std::abs(-2.3)=2.3

Good unit test should be able to catch all this if there are
different behaviors. Otherwise, it's not really unit testable.
For lgamma, the error behavior was different.

I wouldn't worry about deprecation for the moment. Feel
free to just leave fabs() and fmin() and fmax() and change the
doc to indicate they're there for C++ lib compatibility.

- Bob
